newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE - Two years after singer's murder it's Selena, the movie.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Two years after singer's murder it's Selena, the movie.

text.p: Two years after she was gunned down by the former president of her own fan club, "Tejano" singing star Selena is more popular than ever and about to achieve even greater fame.

Just as the Grammy-winning songstress was poised to move before her death from regional Tejano music into mainstream America, Warner Bros. studio believes "Selena" -- the movie -- will be a crossover hit as well. "She was a hybrid of Whitney (Houston) and Janet (Jackson)," said Jose Behar, the record executive who signed her to her first recording contract.

"Selena would have been huge. She was a bicultural artist with persona and an ability to excite the Anglo and Hispanic communities," said Behar of EMI-Latin, which is putting out the original soundtrack of the movie. "Her death expedited her crossover success."

The story of Selena Quintanilla Perez is tailor-made for Hollywood. Pretty young Mexican American girl becomes local star among Hispanic community in southern Texas singing Tejano songs -- a blend of country and Spanish melodies with polka rhythms brought to the region by German immigrants.

On the verge of national stardom, she is murdered in a Corpus Christi motel by Yolanda Saldivar, former president of Selena's fan club, who was accused of embezzlement. Saldivar was found guilty and is serving a life sentence.

Although Selena was a star among teenagers in Texas and other Spanish-speaking parts of America, as well as Mexico, at the time of her death at the age of 23 she had just made her first album in English in country music capital Nashville.
CROSSOVER HIT AFTER DEATH
"Dreaming of You," released posthumously, opened at No. 1 on the Billboard chart in July 1995. Warner Bros. thinks this cross-over appeal will make the movie a big hit across the cultural divide.

"I don't think of it as a Hispanic film," director Gregory Nava told the Los Angeles Times. "The story of Selena is a beautiful story and I've always been a believer that beautiful stories, well-told, are of interest to everybody."

To that end, Warner Bros. is promoting the film in both the Hispanic and the Anglo markets. In select markets with large Hispanic populations, the movie will show in two versions, one in the original and one with Spanish subtitles.
The film opens on Friday, but when it was previewed at a theatre recently in Selena's hometown of Corpus Christi, Texas, Jennifer Lopez, who plays the slain star, was mobbed.

"When I first got the part, I didn't know how they would accept me, the fans," she told Reuters in an interview. "But I walked in and they were screaming and yelling. It was pretty incredible the acceptance I was feeling."
For Lopez, a Puerto Rican actress from New York, who was in "The Money Train" and currently "Blood and Wine" opposite Jack Nicholson, "Selena" could be a breakthrough role.
LOVE AND PASSION SURROUNDED SELENA
"I wasn't as excited about it at first until I started learning about her. That's when I became excited," she said.

"I realised that whoever got the part would be under a lot of scrutiny. There's so much love and passion surrounding Selena, whoever would have got it would have gone through the same thing," said Lopez, who bears such a remarkable resemblance to the singer that she admitted she once mistook one of her own shots from the film for a picture of Selena.
Having been accepted by Selena's fans, Lopez can now look at the implications of the role for her career.

"These kind of film roles don't come along every day for actresses like me. For Latina actresses, it doesn't happen every day," she said. "I don't think a lot of people realise that Latinos in this country, who were born here and whose parents were born here, actually consider ourselves American. And that's something I like about this film."
Like the woman she plays, Lopez did not grow up speaking Spanish. Her immigrant parents believed that to make it in America their children had to speak English.

"Selena was Latin, yes. But she was American (first). I'm an American, you know, even though my parents were born in Puerto Rico. I'm proud of my culture and so was Selena. I embrace it and celebrate it, but I am American," she said.
Like Selena, she had to learn to sing in Spanish, although for the movie Selena's actual voice is dubbed over hers.
